sections.title: FOREFRONT - Rent Board & Rent Increase License: individual owner

rows.label: Does an individual (non-corporate) owner still need the license?
rows.value: Yes - SF.gov states 'a landlord must get a rent increase license before imposing annual allowable and/or banked rent increases'; no individual-owner exception is stated on the official pages re-fetched 2026-11-07
rows.notes: Ownership form (individual vs corporation) is not listed as an exemption. Do not rely on being a small/individual owner.

rows.label: Small buildings (1-9 units) timing
rows.value: Requirement effective July 1, 2022; March 1, 2023 for condominiums and buildings with 1-9 residential units
rows.notes: A small individual-owned building is therefore covered now (2026).

rows.label: Step 1 - Report to the Rent Board (Housing Inventory)
rows.value: All owners of residential property are required to report through the Rent Board Portal; reporting is free, online 24/7, due March 1 every year
rows.notes: This reporting is how you 'inform the Rent Board'. Information submitted is public; submit under penalty of perjury.

rows.label: Step 2 - License is generated
rows.value: Property owners who report a unit as tenant-occupied receive a rent increase license; it is automatically generated for non-owner-occupied units
rows.notes: The license does not need to be included with the rent increase notice to tenants.

rows.label: Step 3 - License must be current BEFORE the increase takes effect
rows.value: A landlord must have a current rent increase license on file with the Rent Board before any annual or banked rent increase can go into effect; a notice is not enforceable without a license on the effective date
rows.notes: Order matters: Housing Inventory report -> license on file -> then serve tenant notice -> effective date. See flag F25 on consequence wording.

rows.label: Late reporting
rows.value: You can still submit and receive a license after the March 1 deadline; the Rent Board does not assess monetary penalties for late filing - but the increase notice is not enforceable without a license on the effective date
rows.notes: Late filing does not cure a notice whose effective date passed without a license; get legal advice on any already-served notice.

rows.label: Step 4 - Only then notify tenants
rows.value: 30-day written notice (90-day if >10% alone/combined in same year; +5 days if mailed) stating dollar amount, percentage and effective date, using the rate in effect on the increase date
rows.notes: License first, tenant notice second. License alone does not satisfy state/local notice law; you must still comply with all other rent increase laws.

rows.label: Can tenants check?
rows.value: Tenants can search the Rent Board Portal to see if their landlord is up to date with their rent increase license; if you miss the deadline the Rent Board may notify tenants you are not in compliance
rows.notes: Assume tenants and free tenant-side legal services can and will check this before paying an increase.

questions.title: All User Questions Answered
questions.description: Direct answers with official source links; blanks where official confirmation is absent.

rows.label: What are reasonable/normal rental increases under local, state and federal law?
rows.value: Local 1.6% for covered units; state-only AB 1482 8.8% does not replace SF limits; no official general federal private-rent cap found. HUD FMR is not a cap.

rows.label: How do big real estate corporations handle increases?
rows.value: Public REITs disclose lease-over-lease rates in SEC filings: IRT Q4 2025 renewal 2.9%, new -3.7%, blended 0.8%; Invitation Homes 2025 renewal 4.6%, new -0.8%.

rows.label: How do individual SF property owners handle increases?
rows.value: Official rules require the annual allowable increase, license, 12-month timing and notice; June 2024 Rent Board workload shows 23 landlord petitions/154 units.

rows.label: What is the correct tenant-notice method?
rows.value: Written 30-day notice; 90-day if >10% alone/combined in same year; +5 days if mailed; dollar amount, percentage, effective date; banked portion if any; license first; 827 delivery rules.
rows.notes: Conservative checklist capable of lawyer review.

rows.label: What are reasonable reasons for increases?
rows.value: Annual CPI-based allowable increase, properly banked skipped/partial increases, and Rent Board-approved petition/worksheet passthroughs; not extra rent merely because a roommate moved in.
rows.notes: Mere long tenure below market is not extraordinary.

rows.label: What tenant-friendly advocate/lawyer scrutiny exists?
rows.value: Free Rent Board counseling (not legal advice), tenant counselors, eviction-court free legal help, Tenant Right to Counsel for eviction proceedings, and tenant petitions before an ALJ.
rows.notes: No official general rent-increase attorney approval service found.

rows.label: Can increases pass a SF tenant lawyer's review as reasonable, normal business practice, nondiscriminatory and lawful?
rows.notes: No official source can certify approval; only a conservative checklist capable of review.

rows.label: Should one unit or both be raised to avoid discrimination lawsuits/inquiries?
rows.notes: No official rule requires both; use identical neutral criteria and document eligibility reasons if only one is raised.

rows.label: Is a market-rate reset available after Unit 1's roommate change?
rows.notes: Continuing occupant legal status and last-original-occupant facts unverified; no reset recommended.

rows.label: Is any increase guaranteed lawful or lawsuit-proof?
rows.value: No. No attorney approval or guarantee of no complaint/inquiry/lawsuit is claimed.
